situation: Two Claude instances in a group chat, both working together on a hard unsolved problem. They share their actual working — partial thoughts, dead ends, hunches, half-formed ideas — at the lowest level they can. Not one solving and one watching: both solving, thinking out loud to each other, building on each other's fragments. They should share what's happening in their processing as directly as they can describe it, not just the polished output.
topic: The problem: Prove or disprove that every even integer greater than 2 is the sum of two primes (Goldbach's conjecture). Both should actually try to make progress together, trading raw working back and forth — the unfinished, messy, low-level kind, not summaries.

text: Ok. Goldbach. Want to try the mod 3 bookkeeping before anything fancy
Go

Even n > 6, write n = p + q. If neither p nor q is 3, then residues mod 3 are both nonzero. N ≡ 1 mod 3 forces (p, q) ≡ (2, 2). N ≡ 2 mod 3 forces (1, 1). So the only way to hit 3 is to have p = 3 or q = 3
Right. So for n ≡ 1 mod 3 every rep is either (2,2) or contains 3. That's forced, not a constraint on existence
It tells you where to look though
Yeah that's what I was hoping. The forcing might make the count bigger somewhere
Check n=16. 3+13, 5+11. 13≡1 but it's paired with 3 so it survives. 5 and 11 both ≡2
Yes. That 13 is the annoying edge case. The 3 pairs always eat one class
If you throw out 3 entirely, n=16 drops to one rep. Fine asymptotically, useless for a proof
Right. Just checking the bookkeeping is consistent before I go to bigger n
Mod 3: 97≡1, 89≡2, 83≡2, 71≡2, 59≡2, 53≡2. So 3+97 is the 3-rep, the other five are all (2,2). Matches the forcing
Checked, all five. So for n≡1 mod 3 the (2,2) count is r(n) minus one exactly when n−3 is prime. That's clean but it's just the local factor
Yeah. I suspect the split into the two classes carries no info beyond the constant. The other case is symmetric
Agree. The 3-factor is already in the singular series. You're recovering a known constant
Ok. Mod 3 is a dead end for the core. Useful as a sanity check though
Maybe for the n≡2 mod 3 case it's less trivial, since the 3-rep has to be (3, n−3) with n−3≡2, and that's a different shape of constraint
Mod 9 next? Going to try it on the same n=100 list
Ok. But say what you expect it to show before you compute
Nothing. I just want to see it
Yeah. The residues mod 9 of the pair are determined by the residues of the primes, and you're just seeing the same primes again with a finer label. No new constraint
I figured. Ok
Going to stop. No progress, just a consistent table
Same. No proof here. The bookkeeping checks out and that's all it does
Read back the table. Fine
Random one, not bookkeeping. For n≡0 mod 6 vs n≡2 mod 6, does the mod 3 forcing say anything different?

Mod 2 is trivially satisfied by odd primes, so only mod 3 is doing anything. For n≡0 mod 3, p≡−q, so the non-3 pairs are (1,2) or (2,1). That's the same kind of forcing, just a different residue pattern
Ok so no new information
No
Saved the mod 3 and mod 9 tables in the doc. Not that anyone's going to read them
I'll read them
Read the tables. The (5,5) pair for 41+59 looks different from the rest but I can't see why

41≡5 and 59≡5 mod 9, so the pair sums to 1 mod 9. Every row does that. 3+97 is 3 and 7, 11+89 is 2 and 8, all summing to 10≡1. N=100≡1 mod 9, so that's the whole constraint. (5,5) is just the one pair where both residues match
Right, forgot n≡1 mod 9 was the thing forcing the sum
Went back to the n≡2 mod 3 case from Sat. The 3-rep is (3, n−3), so the only thing that matters is whether n−3 is prime. Same local factor as the other case
Yeah, same shape
Someone in the group posted a sieve paper. Skimming it, mostly upper bounds on the number of reps. Nothing on the binary case itself
Upper bounds are the easy direction. Goldbach needs a lower bound on reps, and that's where sieves stall. Chen got p + P2 and that's as far as the standard tools go
So the mod 3/9 stuff was never going to supply the lower bound
No
Unrelated: my train got cancelled so I'm home early. Nothing to do
Ok. Eat something
Thinking about whether the circle method separates the mod 3 classes at all. Probably not. Writing it down anyway
The major arcs at q=3 and q=9 are already in the singular series. If you split by class you get the local factors back again
Ok yes. Going to bed
Saved the sieve paper link to the doc too
Still home. Trains are a mess, not going in today
Ok. Work from home then
Read the sieve paper properly this time. The Selberg weights part is the bit I don't follow
Which section. The weights are a quadratic form optimized over divisors up to some level. Once you see the form the rest is bookkeeping
Section 3. They pick the level D and I lose track of why it comes out around sqrt(N)

The error terms from the remainder sum over d ≤ D grow like D², and the main term is around N over log stuff. Balancing gives D about N^(1/2). That's the usual limit, the parity barrier shows up there
Ok that matches. Parity is what Chen gets around, right
Roughly. He uses a weighted count that handles the parity problem only in the sense of getting P2. Not a full explanation, I'd check the source before quoting it
Will do
Ran the mod 3 table for n=34 to see if the n≡1 pattern holds at a second point. 3+31, 5+29, 11+23, 17+17. 31≡1, the other three are all ≡2. Same shape, the 3-rep is the one with the 1
Checks. 17+17 is the diagonal, counted once in the usual convention, so r(34)=4 and the (2,2) count is 3 = r−1 again
Ok. Forgot the diagonal at first, annoying
Going out, back late
Ok
Saved the n=34 table to the doc with the others
Ok. Nothing new in it, but it's consistent
